text: Notebooks are ideal for exploring. But once your cleaning logic works, leaving it buried in cell 47 has real costs — you can't test it, you can't run it on a schedule, and two people can't easily edit it at once. Refactoring means moving the reusable parts into plain Python files while keeping the notebook for what it genuinely does best: exploring and presenting. This lesson takes the orders cleaning logic from last time and turns it into a small, runnable project.

A useful rule of thumb: anything you'd want to run twice, or test, moves out — that usually means loading, cleaning, and feature-building steps. What stays in the notebook is the exploration, the charts, and the narrative explaining what you actually found. The refactoring path has four steps: get the notebook working top to bottom with Restart and Run All, turn repeated or important cells into functions, move those functions into a dot-p-y module, and add a script that wires the functions together.

Here's a simple project layout. A data folder holding the raw CSV. An orders underscore pipeline folder with an empty init file, marking it as an importable package, and a cleaning dot p-y file inside it holding the actual functions. A run underscore pipeline script at the top level. And the analysis notebook, now much shorter, sitting alongside everything else.

Inside cleaning dot p-y, each small function does exactly one job and returns a new DataFrame — standardize underscore region strips whitespace and title-cases the region column, working on a copy so it never mutates its input. Clean underscore orders chains several of these together into one full pipeline — drop duplicates by order id, then dot-pipe into standardize underscore region, then dot-pipe into add underscore revenue. Pipe passes the DataFrame into each function in turn, reading top to bottom like a sentence.

Run underscore pipeline dot p-y wires it all together as a real script. Argparse turns command-line flags into a tidy args object, so file paths are never hard-coded into the script itself — here, an input path and an output path, both required. The if-name-equals-main guard means main only runs when this file is executed directly, so importing it elsewhere, like from a notebook, never triggers it by accident.

Run it straight from the project folder — python run underscore pipeline dot p-y, dash-dash input pointing at the raw CSV, dash-dash output pointing at where the cleaned file should land. With a five-row sample containing one duplicate order, it prints read 5 rows, wrote 4 rows to orders underscore clean dot c-s-v. The output file comes out with cleaned region names and a brand-new revenue column. Using pathlib dot Path for those paths keeps the code working identically on Windows, macOS, and Linux.

Back in the notebook, one cell now replaces dozens — import clean underscore orders from the module, and call it directly on a freshly loaded CSV. This works as long as the notebook runs from the project folder. If you keep editing the module while the notebook stays open, the IPython magics percent load underscore ext autoreload and percent autoreload 2 reload your changes automatically, with no need to restart the kernel each time.

To recap: move anything you'd rerun or test into functions, then into a module. Keep exploration, charts, and commentary in the notebook itself. A script with main, argparse, and the dunder-main guard is repeatable and schedulable. Use pathlib and arguments instead of hard-coded paths. Next, we protect this code with automated tests.
